1→---
name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests
170→
**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers
190→
### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

200→- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
210→  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
220→  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong
230→
Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
240→jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:
250→
- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks
260→
Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
270→  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
280→  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs

The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.

If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.

## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests

**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers

### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong

Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

1→# op-xray-daemon

D-Bus service for managing the Xray proxy daemon lifecycle.

## Overview

This daemon provides a D-Bus interface (`org.opdbus.v1.Xray`) for controlling the xray proxy process. It replaces direct `Command::new("xray")` subprocess spawning with a schema-driven D-Bus service, adhering to the AGENTS.md D-Bus-first architecture rules.

## D-Bus Interface
10→
**Bus Name:** `org.opdbus.v1.plugins`

**Object Path:** `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray`

**Interface:** `org.opdbus.v1.Xray`

### Methods

| Method | Arguments | Returns | Description |
20→|--------|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `Start` | `config_path: String` | `(bool, String)` | Start xray with the specified config file |
| `Stop` | - | `(bool, String)` | Stop the running xray process |
| `Restart` | `config_path: String` | `(bool, String)` | Stop then start xray with new config |
| `Status` | - | `String` | JSON object with running status, pid, config_path |
| `Reload` | - | `(bool, String)` | Send SIGHUP to xray to reload config |
| `GetConfig` | - | `String` | Return current config path or empty string |

### Status JSON Format

30→```json
{
  "running": true,
  "pid": 12345,
  "config_path": "/etc/xray/xray_config.json",
  "uptime_secs": 3600,
  "start_time": "2024-06-05T10:00:00"
}
```

40→## Configuration Path

Xray's live configuration must exist only at this path inside the container:

```
/etc/xray/xray_config.json
```

The static bootstrap is materialized there during boot. A future validated
control-plane generator replaces that same file atomically and asks the bridge
50→to reload Xray; models do not write or reload Xray directly.

## Usage

### Starting the Daemon

```bash
# Run with default config path
op-xray-daemon

60→# Run with explicit config path
op-xray-daemon --config /etc/xray/xray_config.json
```

### Using D-Bus Methods

#### Start xray

```bash
dbus-send --system --dest=org.opdbus.v1.plugins --type=method_call \
70→  /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray org.opdbus.v1.Xray.Start \
  string:"/etc/xray/xray_config.json"
```

#### Check Status

```bash
dbus-send --system --dest=org.opdbus.v1.plugins --type=method_call \
  /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray org.opdbus.v1.Xray.Status
```
80→
#### Reload Config

```bash
dbus-send --system --dest=org.opdbus.v1.plugins --type=method_call \
  /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray org.opdbus.v1.Xray.Reload
```

#### Stop xray

90→```bash
dbus-send --system --dest=org.opdbus.v1.plugins --type=method_call \
  /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray org.opdbus.v1.Xray.Stop
```

## Replacing Direct Subprocess Spawning

Previously, code would spawn xray directly:

```rust
100→// OLD: Direct subprocess spawn (FORBIDDEN per AGENTS.md)
Command::new("xray")
    .arg("-c")
    .arg("/etc/xray/xray_config.json")
    .spawn()
```

Now, use the D-Bus service instead:

```rust
110→// NEW: D-Bus method call (REQUIRED per AGENTS.md)
use zbus::Connection;

let conn = Connection::system().await?;
let proxy = conn.call_method(
    "org.opdbus.v1.plugins",
    "/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray",
    "org.opdbus.v1.Xray",
    "Start",
    &("/etc/xray/xray_config.json",)
120→).await?;
```

## Installation

See `deploy/install-op-xray-daemon.sh` for D-Bus policy and service installation.

## Architecture

- **D-Bus First:** All xray control operations go through D-Bus methods
130→- **Process Lifecycle:** The daemon maintains a handle to the xray child process
- **Signals:** Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT, properly terminating xray
- **Logging:** Structured logging via `tracing`
- **Config Location:** `/etc/xray/xray_config.json` inside the Xray container

## Dependencies

- `xray` binary in PATH
- D-Bus system bus
- tokio runtime
140→

MIT OR Apache-2.0

    <allow send_destination="org.opdbus.v1.plugins"
           send_interface="org.opdbus.v1.Xray"/>
    <allow receive_sender="org.opdbus.v1.plugins"/>
  </policy>

  <!-- Allow specific group members full access -->
  <policy group="opdbus">
    <allow own="org.opdbus.v1.plugins"/>
    <allow send_destination="org.opdbus.v1.plugins"/>
    <allow send_interface="org.opdbus.v1.Xray"/>
    <allow receive_sender="org.opdbus.v1.plugins"/>
  </policy>
</busconfig>
EOF

echo "Created D-Bus policy: ${DBUS_POLICY_DIR}/org.opdbus.v1.Xray.conf"

# Install the binary
BINARY_PATH="${PROJECT_ROOT}/target/release/op-xray-daemon"
if [ ! -f "$BINARY_PATH" ]; then
    echo "Release binary not found, building..."
    cd "$PROJECT_ROOT"
    cargo build --release -p op-xray-daemon
fi

# Copy binary to system location
INSTALL_DIR="/usr/local/bin"
if [ -d /usr/local/sbin ]; then
    INSTALL_DIR="/usr/local/sbin"
fi

install -m 755 "$BINARY_PATH" "${INSTALL_DIR}/op-xray-daemon"
echo "Installed binary to: ${INSTALL_DIR}/op-xray-daemon"

RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR="/etc/runit/sv/op-xray-daemon"
RUNIT_RUNSVDIR="/etc/runit/runsvdir/default"
mkdir -p "$RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR"
cat > "${RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR}/run" << EOF
#!/bin/sh
exec 2>&1
exec ${INSTALL_DIR}/op-xray-daemon
EOF
chmod +x "${RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR}/run"
if [ ! -e "${RUNIT_RUNSVDIR}/op-xray-daemon" ]; then
    ln -s "$RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR" "${RUNIT_RUNSVDIR}/op-xray-daemon"
fi
echo "Created runit service: ${RUNIT_SERVICE_DIR}"

# Reload D-Bus configuration
echo "Reloading D-Bus configuration..."
if [ -x /bin/dbus-send ] || [ -x /usr/bin/dbus-send ]; then
    dbus-send --system --type=method_call --dest=org.freedesktop.DBus \
        /org/freedesktop/DBus org.freedesktop.DBus.ReloadConfig 2>/dev/null || true
fi

echo ""
echo "Installation complete!"
echo ""
echo "Start the daemon with:"
echo "  sv up op-xray-daemon"
echo ""
echo "Test with:"
echo "  dbus-send --system --dest=org.opdbus.v1.plugins --type=method_call /org/opdbus/v1/plugins/xray org.opdbus.v1.Xray.Status"
echo ""

# System One

> Answer one or more questions about the content supplied in `state`.

You can mix question types in one request. Answers use the same names as the
questions, so you can match each result to its question. The response also includes
the model used and token usage.



## OpenAPI

````yaml https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json post /v1/systemone
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: TypeSafe
  description: >-
    Ask yes/no questions, evaluate statements, select choices, or assign ratings
    to your content. Send your API key in the Authorization header as `Bearer
    <API_KEY>`. Use GET /v1/models to discover available model names.
  version: 0.2.0
servers:
  - url: https://api.typesafe.ai
security: []
paths:
  /v1/systemone:
    post:
      summary: System One
      description: >-
        Answer one or more questions about the content supplied in `state`.


        You can mix question types in one request. Answers use the same names as
        the

        questions, so you can match each result to its question. The response
        also includes

        the model used and token usage.
      operationId: systemone_v1_systemone_post
      parameters:
        - name: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images
          in: header
          description: Set to true to use assets or box questions.
          schema:
            type: string
            enum:
              - 'true'
          example: 'true'
        - name: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context
          in: header
          description: Set to true to use long context.
          schema:
            type: string
            enum:
              - 'true'
          example: 'true'
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/SystemOneRequest'
            examples:
              noul:
                summary: Noul
                value:
                  model: jev-latest
                  state: >-
                    I was charged twice for my subscription this month. Please
                    refund the extra charge.
                  questions:
                    billing:
                      type: noul
                      instructions: Is this message about billing?
              choice:
                summary: Choice
                value:
                  model: jev-latest
                  state: >-
                    I was charged twice for my subscription this month. Please
                    refund the extra charge.
                  questions:
                    tone:
                      type: choice
                      instructions: What is the tone of this message?
                      criteria:
                        angry: An upset or hostile message
                        calm: A neutral or polite message
                        excited: An enthusiastic or eager message
              score:
                summary: Score
                value:
                  model: jev-latest
                  state: >-
                    I was charged twice for my subscription this month. Please
                    refund the extra charge.
                  questions:
                    urgency:
                      type: score
                      instructions: How urgent is this message?
                      criteria:
                        - Can wait
                        - Needs attention this week
                        - Needs attention today
              box:
                summary: 'Box (requires TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true)'
                value:
                  model: jev-preview
                  state: photo
                  questions:
                    red_rectangle:
                      type: box
                      instructions: Locate the red rectangle.
                  assets:
                    photo:
                      type: image
                      format: png
                      data_base64: >-
                        iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABAAAAAQCAIAAACQkWg2AAAAHElEQVR4nGP4TyJgoKcGBgbsaFQDfTUQB4aDBgDAen2fpitsVAAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==
          multipart/form-data:
            schema:
              type: object
              description: >-
                The JSON request as the first part, named request, then each
                image as its own part. Every image part needs a unique,
                non-empty name and must be used by exactly one asset's part.
              properties:
                request:
                  description: The JSON request, as the first part.
                  contentMediaType: application/json
                  contentSchema:
                    $ref: '#/components/schemas/SystemOneRequest'
              required:
                - request
              additionalProperties:
                type: string
                description: An image, named by the asset part that uses it.
                contentMediaType: image/*
            encoding:
              request:
                contentType: application/json
        required: true
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful Response
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/SystemOneResponse'
              examples:
                noul:
                  summary: Noul
                  value:
                    model: jev-latest
                    answers:
                      billing:
                        type: noul
                        noul: 0.98
                    usage:
                      input_tokens: 120
                      output_tokens: 12
                choice:
                  summary: Choice
                  value:
                    model: jev-latest
                    answers:
                      tone:
                        type: choice
                        choice: calm
                        confidence: 0.7
                        probabilities:
                          angry: 0.15
                          calm: 0.8
                          excited: 0.05
                    usage:
                      input_tokens: 120
                      output_tokens: 12
                score:
                  summary: Score
                  value:
                    model: jev-latest
                    answers:
                      urgency:
                        type: score
                        score: 1.7
                        confidence: 0.55
                        legend:
                          '0': Can wait
                          '1': Needs attention this week
                          '2': Needs attention today
                        probabilities:
                          '0': 0.1
                          '1': 0.1
                          '2': 0.8
                    usage:
                      input_tokens: 120
                      output_tokens: 12
                box:
                  summary: Box
                  value:
                    model: jev-preview
                    answers:
                      red_rectangle:
                        type: box
                        box:
                          top: 0.2
                          bottom: 0.66
                          left: 0.19
                          right: 0.68
                        confidence: null
                    usage:
                      input_tokens: 285
                      output_tokens: 20
        '422':
          description: Validation Error
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/HTTPValidationError'
      security:
        - HTTPBearer: []
components:
  schemas:
    SystemOneRequest:
      properties:
        model:
          type: string
          title: Model
          description: >-
            Name or alias of the model to use. Available names are returned by
            GET /v1/models.
          examples:
            - jev-latest
        state:
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: State
          description: The content all questions in this request refer to.
          examples:
            - I was charged twice. Please help.
            - message: Please help.
              subject: Duplicate charge
        questions:
          additionalProperties:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Question'
          type: object
          minProperties: 1
          title: Questions
          description: >-
            Questions to ask about the content, each with a name you choose. The
            response uses those names to identify the answers.
          examples:
            - billing:
                instructions: Is this message about billing?
                type: noul
        assets:
          additionalProperties:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Asset'
          type: object
          minProperties: 1
          title: Assets
          description: >-
            Media assets keyed by an opaque placeholder (recommend a per-image
            UUID). Each placeholder, wherever it appears as or inside a string
            in state, question instructions, or criteria, is replaced with the
            asset. Image assets require a vision-language model.
      type: object
      required:
        - model
        - state
        - questions
      title: SystemOneRequest
      description: Content and named questions to evaluate together using a TypeSafe model.
    SystemOneResponse:
      properties:
        model:
          type: string
          title: Model
          description: >-
            Name of the model that answered the questions. May differ from the
            alias supplied in the request.
          examples:
            - jev-latest
        answers:
          additionalProperties:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Answer'
          type: object
          minProperties: 1
          title: Answers
          description: >-
            Answers keyed by the question names supplied in the request. Each
            answer's type matches its question's type.
          examples:
            - billing:
                noul: 0.98
                type: noul
        usage:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/Usage'
          description: Input and output token counts for this evaluation.
          examples:
            - input_tokens: 120
              output_tokens: 12
      type: object
      required:
        - model
        - answers
        - usage
      title: SystemOneResponse
      description: Answers grouped by question name, with the model used and token usage.
    HTTPValidationError:
      properties:
        detail:
          items:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/ValidationError'
          type: array
          title: Detail
          description: >-
            Validation errors describing which request values are missing or
            invalid.
          examples:
            - - loc:
                  - body
                  - state
                msg: Field required
                type: missing
      type: object
      title: HTTPValidationError
      description: Request validation failures returned with HTTP status 422.
    Question:
      oneOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/NoulQuestion'
          title: Noul
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/ChoiceQuestion'
          title: Choice
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/ScoreQuestion'
          title: Score
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/BoxQuestion'
          title: Box
      discriminator:
        propertyName: type
        mapping:
          noul: '#/components/schemas/NoulQuestion'
          choice: '#/components/schemas/ChoiceQuestion'
          score: '#/components/schemas/ScoreQuestion'
          box: '#/components/schemas/BoxQuestion'
      description: A question about the supplied content.
    Asset:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: image
          title: Type
          description: Identifies an image asset.
        format:
          type: string
          enum:
            - png
            - jpg
            - jpeg
          title: Format
          description: >-
            The image format, required with data_base64. The actual format is
            detected from the bytes.
        data_base64:
          type: string
          title: Data Base64
          description: Base64-encoded image data.
        part:
          type: string
          title: Part
          description: >-
            In a multipart request, the name of the image part this asset uses.
            With part, data_base64 is ignored.
      type: object
      title: Asset
      description: >-
        An image that replaces its placeholder: its bytes in data_base64 with
        their format, or, in a multipart request, the name of the image part
        that holds them. Requests with images must send the header
        TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true.
    Answer:
      oneOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/NoulAnswer'
          title: Noul
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/ChoiceAnswer'
          title: Choice
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/ScoreAnswer'
          title: Score
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/BoxAnswer'
          title: Box
      discriminator:
        propertyName: type
        mapping:
          noul: '#/components/schemas/NoulAnswer'
          choice: '#/components/schemas/ChoiceAnswer'
          score: '#/components/schemas/ScoreAnswer'
          box: '#/components/schemas/BoxAnswer'
      description: An answer whose type matches the corresponding question.
    Usage:
      properties:
        input_tokens:
          type: integer
          title: Input Tokens
          description: Number of billable input tokens used to evaluate the request.
          examples:
            - 120
        output_tokens:
          type: integer
          title: Output Tokens
          description: >-
            Number of output tokens used to answer the questions. Output tokens
            are currently free of charge.
          examples:
            - 12
      type: object
      required:
        - input_tokens
        - output_tokens
      title: Usage
      description: Token usage for the request.
    ValidationError:
      properties:
        loc:
          items:
            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - type: integer
          type: array
          title: Location
          description: >-
            Path to the invalid value: the request location followed by field
            names and array indices.
          examples:
            - - body
              - questions
              - urgency
              - score
              - criteria
        msg:
          type: string
          title: Message
          description: Human-readable explanation of the validation failure.
          examples:
            - Field required
        type:
          type: string
          title: Error Type
          description: Machine-readable validation error code.
          examples:
            - missing
        input:
          title: Input
          description: The input value that failed validation.
          examples:
            - type: score
        ctx:
          type: object
          title: Context
          description: Additional context used to explain the validation failure.
          examples:
            - min_length: 1
      type: object
      required:
        - loc
        - msg
        - type
      title: ValidationError
      description: A request validation error at a specific field or array element.
    NoulQuestion:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: noul
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a yes/no question or statement.
          examples:
            - noul
        instructions:
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: Instructions
          description: The yes/no question or statement to evaluate.
          examples:
            - Is this message spam?
            - This message contains unsolicited advertising.
            - task: Identify unsolicited advertising.
        criteria:
          anyOf:
            - $ref: '#/components/schemas/NoulCriteria'
            - type: 'null'
          description: Criteria clarifying what counts as a yes or no answer.
          examples:
            - 'false': A legitimate conversation
              'true': Unsolicited advertising
      type: object
      required:
        - type
      title: NoulQuestion
      description: >-
        A yes/no question or statement, answered with the probability of yes or
        true.
    ChoiceQuestion:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: choice
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a question that selects one of the choices in criteria.
          examples:
            - choice
        instructions:
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: Instructions
          description: What the model should decide when choosing an option.
          examples:
            - What is the tone of this message?
        criteria:
          additionalProperties:
            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - additionalProperties: true
                type: object
              - items: {}
                type: array
              - type: 'null'
            x-accepts: string | object | array
          type: object
          minProperties: 1
          maxProperties: 255
          title: Criteria
          description: >-
            Choice names and descriptions of when each applies. A choice without
            a description is interpreted by its name alone.
          examples:
            - angry: An upset or hostile message
              calm: A neutral or polite message
              excited: An enthusiastic or eager message
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - criteria
      title: ChoiceQuestion
      description: A question that selects one option from the choices you define.
    ScoreQuestion:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: score
          title: Type
          description: >-
            Identifies a question that rates the content using the levels in
            criteria.
          examples:
            - score
        instructions:
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: Instructions
          description: What the model should rate.
          examples:
            - How urgent is this message?
        criteria:
          items:
            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - additionalProperties: true
                type: object
              - items: {}
                type: array
            x-accepts: string | object | array
          type: array
          minItems: 1
          maxItems: 10
          title: Criteria
          description: >-
            Ordered descriptions of the score levels. Each description's
            position determines its score, starting at zero.
          examples:
            - - Can wait
              - Needs attention this week
              - Needs attention today
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - criteria
      title: ScoreQuestion
      description: A question that assigns a score using an ordered rubric.
    BoxQuestion:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: box
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a box question.
        instructions:
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: Instructions
          description: What to locate in the image.
      type: object
      required:
        - type
      title: BoxQuestion
      description: >-
        A question that locates what its instructions describe in the request's
        image. Requests with box questions must send the header
        TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true.
    NoulAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: noul
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a yes/no answer.
          examples:
            - noul
        noul:
          type: number
          title: Noul
          description: >-
            Probability of a yes answer or a true statement, from 0 to 1. Values
            near 1 favor yes or true, values near 0 favor no or false, and
            values near 0.5 indicate uncertainty.
          examples:
            - 0.98
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - noul
      title: NoulAnswer
      description: The probability of a yes answer or a true statement.
    ChoiceAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: choice
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a selection from the requested choices.
          examples:
            - choice
        choice:
          type: string
          title: Choice
          description: >-
            The name of the choice with the highest probability among the
            question's criteria.
          examples:
            - angry
        confidence:
          type: number
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence in the selected choice, from 0 to 1. Higher values
            indicate greater certainty; use lower values to flag uncertain
            selections for review.
          examples:
            - 0.9
        probabilities:
          additionalProperties:
            type: number
          type: object
          title: Probabilities
          description: >-
            Probability of each choice in criteria, keyed by choice name, from 0
            to 1. Shows how likely the alternatives are; values sum to
            approximately 1.
          examples:
            - angry: 0.8
              calm: 0.1
              excited: 0.1
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - choice
        - confidence
        - probabilities
      title: ChoiceAnswer
      description: >-
        The selected choice, confidence, and probabilities for a choice
        question.
    ScoreAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: score
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a rating against the requested score levels.
          examples:
            - score
        score:
          type: number
          title: Score
          description: >-
            Expected score: the probability-weighted average of the rubric
            levels. May fall between integer levels.
          examples:
            - 1.7
        confidence:
          type: number
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence in the score, from 0 to 1. Higher values indicate greater
            certainty; use lower values to flag uncertain ratings for review.
          examples:
            - 0.9
        legend:
          additionalProperties:
            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - additionalProperties: true
                type: object
              - items: {}
                type: array
            x-accepts: string | object | array
          type: object
          title: Legend
          description: >-
            The requested criteria mapped to their score levels, so you can
            interpret the score.
          examples:
            - '0': Can wait
              '1': Needs attention this week
              '2': Needs attention today
        probabilities:
          additionalProperties:
            type: number
          type: object
          title: Probabilities
          description: >-
            Probability of each score level, from 0 to 1, using the same keys as
            legend. Shows how likely the alternatives are; values sum to
            approximately 1.
          examples:
            - '0': 0.1
              '1': 0.1
              '2': 0.8
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - score
        - confidence
        - legend
        - probabilities
      title: ScoreAnswer
      description: >-
        An expected score with its rubric, confidence, and score-level
        probabilities.
    BoxAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: box
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a box answer.
          examples:
            - box
        box:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/BoxCoordinates'
          description: >-
            The box's edges as fractions of image height and width, from 0 to 1.
            Each coordinate is the expected value of its edge's predicted
            position.
          examples:
            - bottom: 0.66
              left: 0.19
              right: 0.68
              top: 0.2
        confidence:
          anyOf:
            - type: number
            - type: 'null'
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence for the given box, from 0 to 1, with 1 being more
            confident. Null when the model does not provide confidence.
          examples:
            - null
            - 0.9
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - box
        - confidence
      title: BoxAnswer
      description: A located box with normalized edge coordinates and confidence.
    NoulCriteria:
      properties:
        'true':
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: 'True'
          description: What counts as a yes answer.
          examples:
            - The message is unsolicited advertising.
        'false':
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: 'False'
          description: What counts as a no answer.
          examples:
            - The message is a legitimate conversation.
      type: object
      title: NoulCriteria
      description: Criteria defining what counts as a yes or no answer.
    BoxCoordinates:
      properties:
        top:
          type: number
          title: Top
          description: >-
            Top edge of the box, as a fraction of image height from the top
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.2
        bottom:
          type: number
          title: Bottom
          description: >-
            Bottom edge of the box, as a fraction of image height from the top
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.66
        left:
          type: number
          title: Left
          description: >-
            Left edge of the box, as a fraction of image width from the left
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.19
        right:
          type: number
          title: Right
          description: >-
            Right edge of the box, as a fraction of image width from the left
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.68
      type: object
      required:
        - top
        - bottom
        - left
        - right
      title: BoxCoordinates
      description: >-
        Normalized box edges. Vertical coordinates are measured from the top of
        the image; horizontal coordinates are measured from the left.
  securitySchemes:
    HTTPBearer:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer

````

# System One

You can mix question types in one request. Answers use the same names as the
questions, so you can match each result to its question. The response also includes
the model used and token usage.



## OpenAPI

  - url: https://api.typesafe.ai
security: []
paths:

        You can mix question types in one request. Answers use the same names as
        the

        questions, so you can match each result to its question. The response
        also includes

        the model used and token usage.
      operationId: systemone_v1_systemone_post
      parameters:
        - name: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images
          in: header
          description: Set to true to use assets or box questions.
          schema:
            type: string
            enum:
              - 'true'
          example: 'true'
        - name: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context
          in: header
          description: Set to true to use long context.
          schema:
            type: string
            enum:
              - 'true'
          example: 'true'
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/SystemOneRequest'
            examples:
              noul:

                value:
                  model: jev-latest
                  state: >-

                  questions:

              choice:

          title: Instructions
          description: What the model should rate.

        criteria:

            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - additionalProperties: true
                type: object
              - items: {}

            x-accepts: string | object | array
          type: array
          minItems: 1
          maxItems: 10
          title: Criteria
          description: >-

      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - criteria
      title: ScoreQuestion

    BoxQuestion:

        instructions:

              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: Instructions
          description: What to locate in the image.
      type: object
      required:
        - type
      title: BoxQuestion
      description: >-
        A question that locates what its instructions describe in the request's
        image. Requests with box questions must send the header
        TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true.
    NoulAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: noul
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a yes/no answer.
          examples:
            - noul
        noul:
          type: number
          title: Noul
          description: >-
            Probability of a yes answer or a true statement, from 0 to 1. Values
            near 1 favor yes or true, values near 0 favor no or false, and
            values near 0.5 indicate uncertainty.
          examples:
            - 0.98
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - noul
      title: NoulAnswer
      description: The probability of a yes answer or a true statement.
    ChoiceAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: choice
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a selection from the requested choices.
          examples:
            - choice
        choice:
          type: string
          title: Choice
          description: >-
            The name of the choice with the highest probability among the

          examples:
            - angry
        confidence:
          type: number
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence in the selected choice, from 0 to 1. Higher values

        probabilities:
          additionalProperties:
            type: number
          type: object
          title: Probabilities

            Probability of each choice in criteria, keyed by choice name, from 0

            approximately 1.
          examples:
            - angry: 0.8

      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - choice
        - confidence
        - probabilities
      title: ChoiceAnswer
      description: >-
        The selected choice, confidence, and probabilities for a choice
        question.
    ScoreAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: score
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a rating against the requested score levels.
          examples:
            - score
        score:
          type: number
          title: Score
          description: >-
            Expected score: the probability-weighted average of the rubric
            levels. May fall between integer levels.
          examples:
            - 1.7
        confidence:
          type: number
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence in the score, from 0 to 1. Higher values indicate greater
            certainty; use lower values to flag uncertain ratings for review.
          examples:
            - 0.9
        legend:
          additionalProperties:
            anyOf:
              - type: string
              - additionalProperties: true
                type: object
              - items: {}
                type: array
            x-accepts: string | object | array
          type: object
          title: Legend
          description: >-
            The requested criteria mapped to their score levels, so you can
            interpret the score.
          examples:
            - '0': Can wait
              '1': Needs attention this week
              '2': Needs attention today
        probabilities:
          additionalProperties:
            type: number
          type: object
          title: Probabilities
          description: >-
            Probability of each score level, from 0 to 1, using the same keys as
            legend. Shows how likely the alternatives are; values sum to
            approximately 1.
          examples:
            - '0': 0.1
              '1': 0.1
              '2': 0.8
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - score
        - confidence
        - legend
        - probabilities
      title: ScoreAnswer
      description: >-
        An expected score with its rubric, confidence, and score-level
        probabilities.
    BoxAnswer:
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
          const: box
          title: Type
          description: Identifies a box answer.
          examples:
            - box
        box:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/BoxCoordinates'
          description: >-
            The box's edges as fractions of image height and width, from 0 to 1.
            Each coordinate is the expected value of its edge's predicted
            position.
          examples:
            - bottom: 0.66
              left: 0.19
              right: 0.68
              top: 0.2
        confidence:
          anyOf:
            - type: number
            - type: 'null'
          title: Confidence
          description: >-
            Confidence for the given box, from 0 to 1, with 1 being more
            confident. Null when the model does not provide confidence.
          examples:
            - null
            - 0.9
      type: object
      required:
        - type
        - box
        - confidence
      title: BoxAnswer
      description: A located box with normalized edge coordinates and confidence.
    NoulCriteria:
      properties:
        'true':
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: 'True'
          description: What counts as a yes answer.
          examples:
            - The message is unsolicited advertising.
        'false':
          anyOf:
            - type: string
            - additionalProperties: true
              type: object
            - items: {}
              type: array
            - type: 'null'
          x-accepts: string | object | array
          title: 'False'
          description: What counts as a no answer.
          examples:
            - The message is a legitimate conversation.
      type: object
      title: NoulCriteria
      description: Criteria defining what counts as a yes or no answer.
    BoxCoordinates:
      properties:
        top:
          type: number
          title: Top
          description: >-
            Top edge of the box, as a fraction of image height from the top

          examples:
            - 0.2
        bottom:
          type: number
          title: Bottom
          description: >-
            Bottom edge of the box, as a fraction of image height from the top

          examples:
            - 0.66
        left:
          type: number
          title: Left
          description: >-
            Left edge of the box, as a fraction of image width from the left
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.19
        right:
          type: number
          title: Right
          description: >-
            Right edge of the box, as a fraction of image width from the left
            (0-1).
          examples:
            - 0.68
      type: object
      required:
        - top
        - bottom
        - left
        - right
      title: BoxCoordinates
      description: >-
        Normalized box edges. Vertical coordinates are measured from the top of
        the image; horizontal coordinates are measured from the left.
  securitySchemes:
    HTTPBearer:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer
